Taking over US Treasury subdomains for $3 each

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Intruder

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone.
  • The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain!
  • As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that elastic IP addresses (EIPs) in AWS are internet routable addresses available for use on cloud systems, by anyone. A common DNS mistake can leave them open for attackers to grab, which can lead to credential theft and worse. We demonstrated the attack is still possible in 2026, including finding real takeovers on US treasury domains, which were reported and fixed via a bug bounty program.

The cost to us for doing this was just $3 per valid takeover - what a bargain! We only covered less than 1% of the total IP space, so there are many more out there for attackers to grab. So, now is the time to review your DNS records and get those dangling records squashed ASAP.

As of the time of writing, the attack still works in practice, and though there are some controls to ban attackers abusing the system, there are sufficient gaps to make the attack practical, and at a reasonable cost.

Recent findings suggest that to test how exploitable it is to claim the AWS host that a dangling DNS record points to, we needed to find a way to cycle through available EIPs with automation. The full EIP space is a maximum of ~80 million IP addresses (in practice, probably half that), and these are allocated at random, so you can’t simply claim the IP address that you want.

To do this, we’d need to repeatedly allocate and release Elastic IPs from AWS’s EC2 pool, and check each address against the DNS records in our scope.

We wanted to report any dangling records we found, so we built our target list from public bug bounty scopes.

Using the bbscope API, we pulled wildcard scope entries and passed them into subfinder to enumerate subdomains. We resolved the A records for each host and stored anything not in private or reserved ranges in a DynamoDB table for use later in our pipeline.

By default, a newly introduced AWS account can hold five Elastic IPs per region. The loop works with five, but a higher quota means more addresses per cycle. Since Service Quotas automatically approves an increase to 25 Elastic IPs per region without a support case, we requested the increase in every region.

With the quota increased, we ran a Python script to claim addresses with each cycle following this flow:.

In a single region, releasing and immediately allocating a upcoming IP often returned the same address, suggesting AWS recycles recently released addresses first. Rotating through regions gave each pool time to move on, so by the time the tool returned to the original region, it would be allocated a fresh set of IPs.

Industry observers note that in just 48 hours, we cycled through 450,000 unique IP addresses before AWS banned the account. This was enough to find 28 live EIP takeovers in the bug bounty scope. We had covered less than 1% of the total EIP space, and already had 28 high impact findings. A determined attacker using a wider scope than bug bounty and running the campaign for an extended period of time would likely find hundreds or even thousands of DNS records that could be hijacked.

Recent findings suggest that after 48 hours, our account received an abuse warning from Amazon with the action “Blocked the ability to allocate and associate Elastic IP in all regions”. This not only stopped us from allocating new IP addresses but also from using our existing matched ones. We wanted to report our findings to customers and bug bounty programs, so we needed to be able to host PoCs on these addresses as evidence the takeover was a success.

Fortunately (or unfortunately depending on how you look at it) AWS allows you to transfer Elastic IPs between accounts, so we created a new account in our testing organization and moved the matching IPs across. It worked without any challenges, despite sitting in the same organization as the banned account. New accounts under an organization can be created without going through the verification process again, so an attacker who gets an account restricted could simply spin up another account and carry on. What was the point of the ban again?

We decided not to continue the full attack from the upcoming account to avoid further abuse complaints, and instead decided to reach out to AWS with some suggestions that could make this attack less practical:.

AWS has since responded. They informed us that they have no plans to change anything here. More on their response in the disclosure section below.

According to recent reports, across our limited target list of bug bounty targets, we were able to claim and control 28 EIPs which matched a live DNS record in the scope, with almost half belonging to government bodies. Bear in mind, we only ran the automation for 48 hours, and we would likely have found more, had we continued.

The most notable were five US Treasury subdomains pointing to addresses we now controlled:.

We also got hits across a range of public bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, including a university, two government bodies, a financial services company, and a large networking vendor. The rest belonged to Intruder customers, who we reported to directly.

In a recent development, once an attacker holds the IP behind a dangling DNS record, they have full control over what that subdomain serves. US government websites tell visitors they can trust a site if its domain ends in .gov and it uses HTTPS - so if an attacker successfully takes over a domain, their site passes the test and customers would trust it without question. The attacker can even pass a certificate authority’s domain validation and get a trusted TLS certificate for the domain to make it look completely legitimate.

Industry observers note that this legitimacy could lead to phishing using a convincing real government domain to steal owners credentials. The attacker could also host services on that domain to gather incoming information, and steal data (e.g. credentials) from any old automations that still point at it. That’s particularly dangerous, since those credentials could provide immediate access to other systems not related to the initial takeover.

In a recent development, AWS publishes 80 million IPv4 addresses for EC2, and our 450,000 allocated IPs cover 0.56% of that space. At our rate of about 9,400 IP addresses per hour, one account would take a year to cycle through every published address.

In a recent development, that’s slow for an attacker with one account. With multiple accounts, it comes down quickly. If bans really do apply only per account, as our experience suggests, 10 accounts could sweep the full space in around five weeks.

According to recent reports, realistically, the acquirable space is much smaller. Much of it is made up of auto-assigned public IPs or addresses held long-term by other customers, so a real sweep would take less time than these figures suggest.

An opportunistic attacker doesn’t need to cover the whole space to find something worth having. Even at 0.56% coverage, we landed 28 subdomains.

Sources indicate that targeting a specific organization narrows the search. An attacker would start by enumerating the target’s subdomains and identifying records that point to unused EC2 addresses. As AWS publishes the region of each range, they can look up exactly which region to search. For a target in eu-west-2, that’s around 2.2 million addresses rather than 80 million. However, when we allocated repeatedly in the same region, we saw a much higher duplicate rate, slowing the search. A targeted attacker therefore has a smaller haystack, but a slower way of searching it.

In a recent development, all findings were reported through the relevant bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure programs, and affected Intruder customers were contacted directly. We also shared our observations on the abuse controls with AWS.

AWS confirmed with us that they don’t plan to make changes, as they see the takeover as depending on customer-side DNS records rather than an issue in their services. They also told us they treat rapid allocation and release as a policy violation and have controls against it. Whilst this is true, they could do more to prevent the issue in our opinion, and the vulnerability class remains open due to their position.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, holo4 is our fresh series of agentic models.
  • Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs.
  • Industry observers note that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, holo4 is our fresh series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Industry observers note that holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

In a recent development, holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

It has been revealed that OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

In a recent development, automationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

In a recent development, the tower is square in initiative at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

Recent findings suggest that A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

In a recent development, our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Industry observers note that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

According to recent reports, our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

It has been revealed that these gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Recent findings suggest that both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.
  • Sources indicate that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018.
  • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

Sources indicate that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Fresh contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] (1 responses).

According to recent reports, the LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It indicates two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

Mental Health AI in 2027: The Human Handoff Becomes the Deciding Feature

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A supportive conversation can make a difficult evening feel less lonely.
  • Industry observers note that mental-health AI in 2027 will be judged increasingly by the service surrounding the conversation.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Dartmouth Therabot trial report describes promising results from a purpose-built, supervised research system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A supportive conversation can make a difficult evening feel less lonely. It can also reach a point where the person needs care the software cannot provide. The quality of the next step—whether someone can actually reach a qualified person—may matter more than how naturally the assistant has been speaking.

Industry observers note that mental-health AI in 2027 will be judged increasingly by the service surrounding the conversation. Evidence, boundaries and human availability will determine whether an approachable interface becomes a useful part of care or a comforting dead end.

Recent findings suggest that the Dartmouth Therabot trial report describes promising results from a purpose-built, supervised research system. It does not establish that general chatbots provide equivalent care or that autonomous treatment is ready for every circumstance. My 2027 forecasts concern evidence, limits and connections to human services. They are assessments of technology and care delivery, rather than treatment recommendations.

According to recent reports, there is a large practical distance between suggesting professional help and helping someone reach it. In 2027, more buyers and clinical evaluations will demand a documented handoff: when it happens, what is transferred and who receives it. A product can be clear about its limits and still fail the person if the promised next step does not exist.

In a recent development, A message recommending professional help is not the same as a functioning transition. A meaningful handoff must account for the service actually available, the information transferred with appropriate permission, and whether somebody takes responsibility for the next step.

It has been revealed that the FDA's Digital Health Advisory Committee material includes consideration of generative-AI mental-health devices. The committee's executive summary highlights evidence and monitoring questions. Advisory discussion is not a product approval or a final rule.

In a recent development, different products will have different roles: a wellness tool, clinician-support system and regulated treatment device should not be assumed to provide the same service. A clear boundary is useful only if the user can understand it at the moment it matters.

Look for tested handoff completion, service availability and the handling of failed connections. Independent evaluations using difficult scenarios would strengthen the forecast. A static disclaimer, or a promise of clinician involvement without staffing and response arrangements, would be much weaker evidence.

Industry observers note that budget for the human service that supports the product. Health systems and employers should ask who receives an escalation and when. A vendor's unit economics should include appropriate support costs, rather than assuming every conversation can end inside the automated interface.

Recent findings suggest that A person may return to an app because it helps, because they are distressed or because nothing else is available. Engagement alone cannot tell those stories apart. In 2027, prospective studies will more clearly specify whom the intervention is for, what it is compared with and which benefits and harms are measured. That will make a smaller, well-supported claim more valuable than broad reassurance.

Frequent use can indicate helpful access, but it can also reflect unresolved distress or dependence on a conversational system. Engagement therefore cannot stand in for symptom improvement, functioning or safety. A convincing evaluation asks whether the tool helps the intended population under the conditions in which it will be offered.

It has been revealed that the Therabot investigators' account is valuable partly because it places the result within a specific trial. The FDA's 2026 generative-AI device discussion paper identifies unresolved regulatory questions; it explicitly does not implement a new policy.

Sources indicate that product design, clinical oversight and study eligibility can change the result substantially. A positive average effect may coexist with poor results for a subgroup or an unacceptable safety signal.

Industry observers note that look for prospectively specified outcomes, attrition, comparison care and subgroup limitations. Longer follow-up and transparent adverse-event reporting would strengthen the evidence. Comparisons with historical therapy results should not be mistaken for a direct trial against qualified clinicians.

Sources indicate that match commercial claims to the exact evidence. Purchasers should check whether trial participants resemble the people who will use the service. A product supported for one condition or supervised setting should not silently expand its claims to every mental-health need.

A familiar interface can conceal a changed intervention. An update may alter advice, tone or responses to ambiguous statements while the product's name stays the same. In 2027, providers and clinical partners will describe more explicit checks before and after material model changes. The continuity that matters is continuity of evidence and behavior, rather than continuity of branding.

In a recent development, A clinical study evaluates a particular intervention. If the underlying conversational model changes, tone, advice, refusal behavior and the handling of ambiguous statements can change as well. Keeping the brand name and interface constant does not guarantee that the studied intervention remains intact.

In a recent development, the FDA's request for feedback on generative-AI devices and advisory materials show why lifecycle evidence matters. These discussions should not be presented as an automatic authorization pathway for a particular product.

It has been revealed that the challenge is that scripted tests cannot cover every conversation. They need to be combined with appropriate monitoring and a process for investigating unexpected behavior without compromising confidentiality.

Industry observers note that look for version-specific evaluation summaries and examples of updates delayed or changed after review. A general commitment to safety is less informative than release criteria. Silent reliance on a third-party model revision would weaken confidence in continuity of the evidence.

Sources indicate that require notification of material changes and clarify who evaluates them. Health-service contracts should preserve a route to pause or replace the tool. Product teams need clinical and operational review capacity that continues after launch, rather than ending when the initial study is published.

People can consent to receiving support without intending to donate their most personal conversations to another purpose. In 2027, more products will clarify those choices separately. Trust will depend on whether declining secondary use is understandable and practical, and whether the actual data flow respects the boundary the person thought they had set.

In a recent development, people can reveal deeply personal information to a responsive conversational interface. They may understand that the service needs to process a message without realizing that the same material could be retained or reused for a different purpose. A warm interface does not remove that distinction.

Recent findings suggest that the FDA discussion paper is a useful starting point for thinking about evolving device practices, but the precise privacy obligations depend on the product, organization and jurisdiction. It would be inaccurate to assume every wellness app is governed in exactly the same way as a health-system record.

In a recent development, I expect clearer product choices because trust is an operating requirement for these services. This is not a prediction that consent language alone will solve the problem. Users also need comprehensible retention periods, access controls and realistic deletion information. A nominal choice that prevents meaningful use of the service may provide little practical agency.

Sources indicate that look for separate, understandable controls and a clear explanation of what changes when a person declines secondary use. Independent review of the actual data flow would strengthen confidence. Broad language buried in a long policy would not demonstrate the predicted improvement.

Map the data flow before choosing a provider, including subcontractors and model services. Give employees or patients an honest account of who can see what. Trust is easier to preserve when the product's behavior matches the choice presented to the user.

Mental-health technology enters a relationship where responsiveness can feel deeply personal. That makes the surrounding obligations especially crucial. The strongest products in 2027 will know their role, show the evidence for it and connect people to human services when the conversation reaches the edge of what software can responsibly provide.

Lila Rowan is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering the intersection of artificial intelligence, healthcare, and mental wellness. Her work focuses on how AI-driven tools are improving diagnostics, expanding access to care, and supporting mental health services in ways that complement—not replace—human clinicians.

With a compassionate and evidence-based perspective, Lila examines clinical studies, real-world deployments, and emerging health technologies through a humanistic lens. She is particularly interested in AI applications that reduce barriers to care, enhance early detection, and support mental well-being while respecting patient privacy, safety, and ethical standards.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus WebAudio nodes, image inputs, and more!

Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a fresh record)!

Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!

We’ve shipped new web platform features:.

According to recent reports, flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640). Example.

We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub problems.

According to recent reports, with respect to accessibility in Servo, we report many more ARIA roles for DOM elements (@alice, @mrobinson, #48839). These can be inspected with the Get Computed Role WebDriver command (@lolaodelola, #47339). Accessibility integration can be turned on with the accessibility_enabled preference.

WebGL2 support received lots of attention this month, with fixes to getParameter(), drawBuffers(), readBuffers(), vertexAttribIPointer(), DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT, getUniformLocation(), vertexAttrib4x(), pixelStorei(), texStorage2D(), texStorage3D(), texImage3D(), getInternalformatParameter(), blitFramebuffer(), and texSubImage2D() (@mxmgorin, #48651, #48620, #48678, #48689, #48751, #48681, #48911, #48972, #48590, #49201, #49289, #48560, #48571). The feature remains gated behind the dom_webgl2_enabled preference.

Sources indicate that reading and writing mapped WebGPU buffers got a significant speed increase (@sagudev, @jdm, #48372). WebGPU can be enabled with the dom_webgpu_enabled preference.

JS script compilation can now occur off the main thread when the dom_script_asynch preference is enabled (@Gae24, #45687). Right now this only applies to non-module scripts.

Recent findings suggest that initial support for the backdrop-filter property has merged (@shubhamg13, #48829). This can be enabled with the layout_css_backdrop_filter_enabled preference.

ServiceWorkers now fire the statechange event when changing states during initialization (@gterzian, #48749). ServiceWorkerContainer can listen for message and messageerror events (@gterzian, #48680). Service Workers remain gated behind the dom_serviceworker_enabled preference.

In a recent development, the Geolocation API has been implemented (@webbeef, #48406). No platform-specific backends to provide the device geolocation data have merged yet, so it remains disabled behind the dom_geolocation_enabled preference.

Recent findings suggest that DOM interfaces for MathML elements now exist, gated behind the mathml_core_enabled preference (@tannal, #48631). There is no MathML-specific layout implemented yet.

Recent findings suggest that A latest, native SVG implementation is in progress (@mu-mostafa98, @jdm, #48467). This work is still in the early stages, but is intended to replace Servo’s dependency on the resvg crate to better integrate with page styling and animations.

IndexedDB cursors now support the revision() and delete() methods (@kuntal-devrat, #48402). The feature can be enabled with the dom_indexeddb_enabled preference.

Support for LargestContentfulPaint performance timing improved, with image URLs (@shubhamg13, #48668), the loadTime value (@shubhamg13, #48676), ignoring non-paintable elements (@shubhamg13, #48856, #48898), video URLs (@shubhamg13, #48931), and following containing blocks (@shubhamg13, #48551). This work is behind the largest_contentful_paint_enabled preference.

We added support for a new performance timing metric: ContainerTiming (@jasonwilliams, #46966). This can be enabled with the container_timing_enabled preference.

Recent findings suggest that our support for adoptedStylesheets improved along with a latest implementation of the ObservableArray specification concept (@jerensl, @arihant2math, #48506). This is right now hidden behind the dom_adoptedstylesheet_enabled preference.

It has been revealed that the Android Compose migration is complete, and embedders now only need to interact with the Servo library component (@veyndan, #48592, #48601, #48595, #48574, #48609, #48778, #48780, #49266). Embedders no longer need to trigger the soft keyboard display; this is controlled by a parameter to the Servo component (@veyndan, #48757).

There’s a new API method to report the network status of the embedder: NetworkManager::set_online_state (@xbwwj, #47568). This data is exposed via the onLine property of the Navigator interface in web content.

Embedders can now disable all support for developer tools, which can reduce the size of the final binary (@janeoa, #47255). This is controlled by the devtools feature and enabled by default; it is also part of the upcoming default_tooling feature.

According to recent reports, customers of the C API can set preferences that accept f64 and f64 array parameters (@fran6co, #49325), as well as the HiDPI scale factor for each WebView (@fran6co, #49327). WebViews can also be resized via the C API (@fran6co, #49326).

The layout_grid_enabled preference has been removed, since CSS Grid now defaults to enabled (@Loirooriol, #48718). Several preferences were renamed (@nicoburns, #48915):.

Double and triple clicking on selected text will extend the selection to the current word and line, respectively (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #48767).

Clicking a link with the middle mouse button now opens up the link in a newly introduced WebView (@SteveSharonSam, @mrobinson, #46000).

Range inputs can be dragged with the mouse (@webbeef, #48342).

Command+delete on macOS will delete the preceding line in a text control (@dzfrias, #48781).

The developer tools continue to improve:.

We improved exception error messages related to the XMLHttpRequest, History, Range, Selection, Element, CharacterData, and DOMTokenList interfaces, and namespaces and attributes (@gabrielecabrini, #49146, #49145, #48786, #49102).

Media elements that start playing outside of a document will no longer be garbage collected until playback finishes (@sabbCodes, @jdm, #49367, #48979).

Pinch zoom operations no longer have to rebuild a full display list, making zooming complex pages much smoother (@stevennovaryo, @mrobinson, #43561).

In a recent development, we improved performance in many small and focused ways by doing less work during restyling and layout (@SimonSapin, @webbeef, @nicoburns, @mrobinson, #49137, #49100, #48485, #48968), reducing GC interactions (@mrobinson, @jschwe, #48984, #49140, #49195, #49425), and delaying work on disconnected trees (@SimonSapin, #49098). We also fixed instances of quadratic layout with deep nesting (@nicoburns, #49148) and missing caching (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #49164, #49073).

We fixed some intermittent GC panics when notifying ResizeObservers (@mrobinson, #49189), introspecting keyframes (@MohamedAli00949, #48546), setting timers (@jdm, #48548), using writable streams (@jdm, #48656), and scrolling iframes after removing them (@mrobinson, #49230).

We also fixed numerous other panics and crashes in scrollable and incremental layout (@mrobinson, #49230, #49283), moving nodes around (@mrobinson, #49226), using WebGPU from opaque origins (@gabrielecabrini, #49207), stringifying some WebIDL types (@mrobinson, #49374), using readable streams (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #49311), clicking disabled file controls (@mrobinson, #49379), rendering giant SVGs (@sabbCodes, #49264), unminifying JS (@jdm, #48567), measuring text (@mxmgorin, #48621), rendering text tracks (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48827), preparing dialogs (@lukewarlow, #49431), and running delayed tasks in destroyed documents (@mrobinson, @jdm, #49399, #48714).

Sources indicate that many small-to-medium improvements to reduce allocations were merged (@yezhizhen, @Narfinger, @Taym95, @mrobinson, @Loirooriol, @CynthiaOketch, @sabbCodes, @mxmgorin, #48549, #48558, #48568, #48598, #48615, #48565, #48646, #48654, #48569, #48562, #48588, #48650, #48702, #48675, #48589, #48720, #48721, #47720, #48745, #48703, #48750, #48770, #48789, #48754, #48828, #48838, #48836, #48841, #48843, #48867, #48882, #48842, #48881, #48840, #48899, #48924, #48904, #48949, #48953, #48980, #49028, #48885, #49035, #49038, #49084, #49131, #49125, #48951, #49154, #49160, #49198, #49202, #49194, #49219, #49258, #49275, #49295, #49298, #49300, #49320, #49323, #49313, #49373, #49380, #48969, #48991). We also reduced memory usage by shrinking some types (@Narfinger, @webbeef, #48954, #48082, #48906).

#115352. Industry News: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1829 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this blueprint includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern indicates up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

In a recent development, provenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a fresh setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

It has been revealed that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

According to recent reports, the most direct result is this: experts mentioned 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

Sources indicate that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

Recent findings suggest that we also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

It has been revealed that blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

Sources indicate that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Recent findings suggest that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Sources indicate that want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval notes "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

In a recent development, hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

According to recent reports, I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Recent findings suggest that hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

Sources indicate that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce fresh errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

Recent findings suggest that the openSUSE Project has been working on the Agama installer for four years; it was the default installer for openSUSE Leap 16.0 when it was released in 2025, and has been adopted by other openSUSE flavors as well. Now the project is gearing up to go all-in on Agama for Tumbleweed, the rolling-release edition that is meant to be where updates and new features land first. Even so, the community has concerns about losing some of YaST's legacy functionality and the impact on installing Tumbleweed on systems that have less RAM.

Cloudflare Debuts Automatic Website Search for AI Agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that cloudflare debuted Search for Agents on November 25, 2026, making the beta feature available on every plan, including Free.
  • Sources indicate that previously, customers had to manually create and configure an AI Search instance, integrate its search endpoints with their domain and tell agents where to find the index.
  • Cloudflare advertises the endpoint on every page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that cloudflare debuted Search for Agents on November 25, 2026, making the beta feature available on every plan, including Free. A dashboard toggle or API control now automates website indexing and exposes an API that AI agents can discover under the site’s own domain.

Sources indicate that previously, customers had to manually create and configure an AI Search instance, integrate its search endpoints with their domain and tell agents where to find the index. For a domain already onboarded to Cloudflare, activation creates the instance and starts crawling and indexing; once indexed, content is searchable at /.well-known/search. The setup documentation instructs customers to index only content they intend to make publicly searchable.

Cloudflare advertises the endpoint on every page. HTML responses carry metadata in their containing agent instructions, the endpoint, the GET method and a documentation link. Sites that also enable Markdown for Agents provide equivalent YAML front matter to agents requesting Markdown. An agent can therefore discover the search capability from a page instead of needing prior knowledge of the site’s index.

Agents submit keywords or natural-language questions through the GET q parameter. Responses contain retrieved Markdown with source references and relevance scores, not an answer generated by another model. Cloudflare’s design leaves synthesis with the agent’s own model and user conversation, so the website supplies source material rather than taking over the response.

Recent findings suggest that cloudflare’s OpenCode demonstration demonstrated an agent discovering the endpoint on the company’s developer-documentation homepage, asking about Cloudflare Artifacts and returning a correct answer a few seconds later. Access remains subject to the domain’s bot-management, AI Crawl Control and Web Application Firewall settings, so the discovery metadata does not bypass existing security controls.

Industry observers note that fresh instances use Discover crawling, which finds pages through sitemaps and links without requiring a sitemap. The defaults crawl five link hops deep, synchronize every 24 hours and exclude subdomains. Search combines vector and keyword retrieval using the @cf/qwen/qwen3-embedding-0.6b embedding model, returns up to 10 chunks and starts with reranking and query rewriting disabled. Similarity caching is enabled for 48 hours.

The embedding model and data source are fixed when the instance is created, though other configurable settings can be changed later. Because the feature uses a standard AI Search instance, owners can also enable public REST or MCP endpoints, access it through a Workers binding or embed search components for human visitors. Those additions are separate and are not required for agent search.

According to recent reports, alongside GET, the endpoint accepts HTTP QUERY requests containing either UTF-8 plain text or a JSON object with a q field. RFC 10008, published in June 2026 and coauthored by Cloudflare’s James M. Snell, defines QUERY as a safe, idempotent way to put query criteria in a request body. Unlike POST, it can be automatically retried without concern for partial state changes, and its responses are cacheable.

Usage is metered across content ingestion, index storage and queries. AI Search billing begins December 1, 2026, and the limits and pricing documentation lists monthly account allowances of 5 million ingestion tokens, 10 GB-month of storage, 1,000 semantic queries and 1,000 full-text queries. Overage rates are $0.75 per million base-ingestion tokens, $2.00 per GB-month of storage, $0.75 per 1,000 semantic, vector or hybrid queries, and $0.10 per 1,000 full-text queries.

According to recent reports, crawl allowances add another constraint. Discover crawling accepts up to 100,000 pages, but per-instance file limits and daily crawl ceilings also apply; the lowest applicable limit determines the resulting page count. On Workers Free, the daily ceiling is 500 pages, making it the binding constraint despite the larger crawl allowance.

The launch makes website retrieval part of Cloudflare’s network configuration instead of a custom integration. Its practical value depends on agents acting on the discovery metadata and on site owners aligning public-content, access and crawl settings. Those choices determine how much useful material an agent can retrieve without crawling pages individually.

Latest Update: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting owners with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an notable gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

Sources indicate that the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

Sources indicate that for streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

According to recent reports, the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

The goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

According to recent reports, we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Concerns and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

According to recent reports, open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let consumers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an key part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as upcoming TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

GitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nexent Capital IFSC Private Limited remarked in a November 25, 2026 announcement that it had debuted Nexent Capital ADGM Fund I, a closed-end fund targeting US$1 billion in capital commitments for quantum-ready AI infrastructure and advanced energy, with a US$20 million anchor commitment from the Tyagi family office.

Industry observers note that the target is not capital already raised. The fund can expand to a US$1.6 billion hard cap and is aimed at institutional and family-office investors, with a minimum investment of US$500,000.

The mandate spans five strategies: infrastructure private equity in AI and data-center assets; private credit and structured capital; special-situations mergers and acquisitions; growth equity and private investments in public equity, or PIPEs; and liquid public-equity exposure within the AI and data-center value chain. The mandate consequently covers the financing and ownership of physical infrastructure as well as investments in companies across that value chain.

Nexent noted it has line of sight to an identified pipeline across North America and India, including data-center and power assets sponsored by affiliates of the Nexent Capital and Tryfacta platform. These are pipeline projects, not acquisitions the fund has completed.

Director Abhimanyu Tyagi described the pipeline as drawing on relationships and projects the platform had developed for years, ranging from data-center conversions to gigawatt-scale energy campuses.

Managing partner Adesh Tyagi framed the investment case around AI’s physical requirements: “AI is being built on a foundation of physical infrastructure — power, land, and compute — that most capital isn’t positioned to finance at the scale or speed this moment demands.”.

The structure comprises an Abu Dhabi Global Market (ADGM)-domiciled Qualified Investor Fund as the master fund, with a GIFT City-based Alternative Investment Fund regulated by IFSCA acting as its feeder. Nexent Capital ADGM Limited is being established as the licensed ADGM fund manager.

Nexent is working with an Abu Dhabi-based fund administrator that it says manages more than US$3.4 trillion in assets globally. Formal engagement of legal counsel and an auditor is progressing as part of the path to FSRA authorization.

The fund has not yet received that authorization. Nexent targets a first close approximately six months after FSRA authorization and a final close six months later, so neither closing has occurred.

The launch sets out a cross-border financing route aimed at the physical requirements of AI expansion. Its practical scale will depend on securing authorization, raising the targeted commitments and converting the identified pipeline into investments. For now, the announcement represents prospective infrastructure financing rather than new operating data-center or energy capacity.

#115344. Latest Update: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2032 w)
