Breaking: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
  • A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
  • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and fresh Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

In a recent development, you'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

In a recent development, FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

In a recent development, every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

It has been revealed that A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The fresh Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

It has been revealed that the decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

Recent findings suggest that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

In a recent development, audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them upcoming paths through Metal:.

It has been revealed that token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

Sources indicate that you can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

Recent findings suggest that several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Sources indicate that work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

In a recent development, once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

According to recent reports, scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A major thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

Guilherme Joventino, Co-Founder & COO of MIGNOW – Interview Series

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2536 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, guilherme Joventino is Co-Founder and COO of MIGNOW.
  • Recent findings suggest that MIGNOW develops proprietary software that uses AI and machine learning to automate SAP migration, upgrades, and ongoing modernization.
  • Industry observers note that you’ve worked on global SAP teams at Philips, Sandoz, and Bayer before co-founding MIGNOW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, guilherme Joventino is Co-Founder and COO of MIGNOW. His background includes work on global SAP teams at Philips, Sandoz, and Bayer. At MIGNOW, he focuses on making enterprise modernization more predictable through phased delivery, automation, and continuous system evolution, while retaining the business expertise and accountability needed for critical ERP environments.

Recent findings suggest that MIGNOW develops proprietary software that uses AI and machine learning to automate SAP migration, upgrades, and ongoing modernization. Its approach combines strategy and planning, technical conversion, stabilization, and continuous evolution, with tools for assessing legacy environments and moving toward SAP S/4HANA and a cleaner, more adaptable core.

Industry observers note that you’ve worked on global SAP teams at Philips, Sandoz, and Bayer before co-founding MIGNOW. What recurring challenges convinced you that enterprise modernization needed a different approach?

Industry observers note that one pattern kept repeating. Companies kept adding “what ifs” to their SAP projects. What if we also redesign this process? What if we add this new requirement? What if we solve that old problem while we’re at it? Each idea made sense on its own, but together they turned migrations into huge projects that were very hard to predict. Timelines slipped, budgets grew and everything rested on one high-risk go-live.

Scale made this worse. When SAP revealed the end of mainstream maintenance for ECC, it became clear the market couldn’t keep working this way. Around 40,000 SAP ECC customers worldwide need to move to SAP S/4HANA, and the industry doesn’t have enough specialists to run that many complex, manual projects.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why we see transformation as a series of clear, measurable phases rather than one big event. You start with the destination, then move step by step. Each phase has a defined scope, so the organization always knows where it stands and what comes next. A predictable process carries less risk, and it starts delivering value sooner.

For readers who are less familiar with enterprise software, how can an aging SAP system limit a manufacturer’s AI ambitions, and which limitations are hardest to overcome?

It has been revealed that I usually compare it to a smartphone that hasn’t been updated in ten years. It still makes calls, but the newly introduced apps don’t run on it.

Recent findings suggest that an older SAP ERP keeps the business running, but it wasn’t built for the way AI works today. SAP’s newest AI capabilities, such as Joule and SAP Business AI, are designed for SAP S/4HANA and the cloud. On top of that, many legacy environments are hard to integrate. One IT leader we worked with put it simply: before the migration, every time the business asked to integrate something, the answer was “we can’t.”.

It has been revealed that technology isn’t the hardest limitation to overcome. Accumulated complexity is. Years of custom code, poorly documented business logic and data spread across different structures make it difficult for any AI tool to understand what the system is doing. AI is only as useful as the environment it works in. If the foundation is fragmented, AI just makes that complexity move faster.

It has been revealed that what does making an SAP environment “AI-ready” actually involve beyond migrating to the cloud? How do you assess whether its data, integrations, and business processes can support useful AI applications?

Moving to the cloud changes where the system runs. It doesn’t automatically change how ready the system is. For me, an AI-ready SAP environment has four characteristics: a current version of SAP S/4HANA, a core that is as clean and standard as possible, reliable data and integrations that work through modern interfaces instead of point-to-point workarounds.

Clean Core is a central part of this. When customizations are kept outside the core, the system can receive SAP’s updates and innovations, including AI features, without breaking what the business built over the years.

Our assessment starts before any conversion. In the first phase of our methodology, we use our own AI-powered tools to analyze the current landscape: what is customized, what is actually used, where the critical gaps are and which dependencies could create risk. That gives the organization a factual picture of its environment and a roadmap based on its real system, not on assumptions or deadlines.

Could you walk us through how MIGNOW modernizes a legacy SAP environment, explaining where you use AI, where you rely on rules-based automation, and where human expertise remains essential?

Our methodology has four phases: strategy and planning, technical conversion, stabilization and continuous evolution. Each one has its own goals and deliverables.

Sources indicate that our AI is based on machine learning. It learns what worked in previous projects and applies that knowledge to new ones. In practice, this means that in our case AI and rules-based automation aren’t really separate things. Everything our AI automates follows the same rules and patterns, consistently, because those patterns come from hundreds of real projects. Every new project makes the next one more accurate.

Recent findings suggest that human expertise comes in mainly where an environment has a very high volume of complex custom code. Even there, depending on what the code does, our AI can often automate much of the work. At Eternit, for example, 11,535 of 11,652 custom code objects were adapted automatically, and only 117 required manual work.

People are also essential to the decisions around the conversion: understanding what the business needs, validating results with key consumers and owning the go-live. Automation removes repetitive work. It doesn’t remove accountability.

Industry observers note that years of custom code often capture business logic that is poorly documented. How does your technology determine what to preserve, rewrite, or retire—and verify that automated changes maintain the intended behavior?

Recent findings suggest that our view is that the business logic should be preserved, but not the code exactly as it was written. Instead, we update and optimize custom code so it performs the same functions using SAP’s more modern tools, such as SAP BTP and other current technologies.

Sources indicate that keeping custom code exactly as it is can feel safer in the short term, but it leaves the system “dirty.” Every customization built directly into the core makes future upgrades slower, riskier and more expensive. In the end, the firm is moving its technical debt to a upcoming platform instead of solving it.

That’s the idea behind our Clean Core solution. Our AI, trained on hundreds of projects, identifies the changes that pull the system away from SAP’s standard and recreates outdated objects using models SAP recommends. That can mean turning older reports into SAP Fiori apps, moving RFC interfaces to OData services or moving PI/PO integrations to Cloud Integration on SAP BTP. In SAP’s terms, we turn low-maturity legacy code into extensions aligned with the Tier 1 and Tier 2 models SAP recommends.

Verification is part of the process. The solution generates tests and technical documentation for each change, which supports audits and governance. The results are then validated in non-production environments, with the business areas involved, before anything reaches production.

The goal goes beyond a successful migration. We want a system that is easier to evolve every time SAP releases something new.

With mainstream maintenance for SAP Business Suite 7 core applications ending in 2027 and optional extended maintenance available through 2030, how should companies weigh the cost of waiting against the risks of rushing a migration?

I don’t think the real choice is between waiting and rushing. The real choice is between planning on your own terms and reacting to a deadline.

Recent findings suggest that extended maintenance buys time, but it comes at an additional cost, and it doesn’t solve the underlying problem. Meanwhile, technical debt keeps growing, the system falls further behind and the company postpones its access to new SAP capabilities, including AI.

There is also a capacity concern that I think many companies underestimate. Tens of thousands of companies still need to migrate, while the market can deliver only a few thousand projects per year. As 2027 and 2030 get closer, specialists become scarcer and more expensive.

In a recent development, one of our clients mentioned it very clearly: the longer you postpone this decision, the worse it gets. My recommendation is to start with a solid assessment now. Once you understand your landscape, you can move at a pace that is safe for your business instead of one dictated by the calendar.

Could you share a concrete example from your work with Carrefour or Eternit, including the original challenge, measurable results, and whether the modernization enabled any AI capabilities that were previously difficult to deploy?

Two projects show different sides of this.

Carrefour Brasil came to us with a very specific challenge. They wanted to move from SAP ECC to SAP S/4HANA through RISE with SAP and be live in time for Black Friday, which is the most vital date for retail e-commerce in Brazil. Other proposals had estimated about 18 months. We completed the project in three and a half months, converting 7,566 objects with 99.3% automation, and the latest environment supported Carrefour’s transaction volumes during Black Friday. With SAP S/4HANA in place, Carrefour could start delivering new functionalities and technologies to the business, including recommendation capabilities based on historical data.

Industry observers note that eternit, a leading Brazilian building materials organization, had a different situation: an outdated SAP version, two separate SAP environments that needed to be unified into one instance, several parallel subprojects and a lean team. Working with Seidor and AWS, we completed a Shell conversion in 11 months with about 99% automation of custom code. The go-live was smooth. Within a day and a half, the company was invoicing normally, and the project closed with zero escalations. Eternit was also ready for Brazil’s tax reform.

Recent findings suggest that to be precise about AI: in Eternit’s case, the migration removed the barrier rather than delivering AI on day one. Their team is now working on Clean Core and identifying AI quick wins to reduce operational workload, something the old environment simply couldn’t support.

It has been revealed that when AI is involved in changing systems that support finance, inventory, or procurement, errors can have significant consequences. What testing, audit trails, and human approval processes do you use before changes reach production?

I agree completely. In an ERP, a small error can affect invoicing, inventory or a company’s financial statements, so speed can never come at the expense of control.

It has been revealed that that’s why we developed our own methodology, inspired by SAP’s methodology and supported by professionals with more than a decade of SAP experience. Every project follows clear phases, and nothing goes directly to production. Changes move through SAP’s standard landscape, from development to quality assurance and only then to production, which gives every change traceability. The key consumers from each business area test their own processes before go-live, because they are the people who know whether a result is actually correct.

The go-live itself is a planned, joint decision with the client, with clear acceptance criteria and a contingency plan. After the project, we have a dedicated hypercare period to monitor the environment and resolve issues before they affect operations.

For me, the role of AI in this process is to give people better information and remove repetitive work, not to replace their approval. The more critical the process, the more important it is that a person with business knowledge signs off.

As enterprises explore AI agents that can take actions inside business systems, what safeguards are needed around data access, permissions, and transaction execution—and how should modernization prepare for them?

An AI agent inside an ERP shouldn’t just be capable of taking action. We need to know exactly what it can access, what it’s allowed to change and how every action is monitored and audited.

According to recent reports, in practice, that means applying the same principles we already use for people, and making them stricter: least-privilege access, clear authorization profiles, approval steps for sensitive transactions and complete logs of what the agent did and why. Companies also need to know where their data is processed and which models they are using, especially in regulated industries.

It has been revealed that modernization is what makes these safeguards possible. In a legacy environment full of undocumented customizations, it’s very hard to define clear boundaries, because nobody knows exactly what each piece of code does. A current, cleaner SAP environment with well-defined processes and permissions gives AI agents a safe space to operate. The more autonomy we give these systems, the more the foundation matters.

According to recent reports, looking ahead three to five years, do you expect SAP modernization to become a continuous, increasingly autonomous process? What technical or organizational barriers still need to be solved for that vision to become practical?

Recent findings suggest that yes, I believe that’s where the market is going, and it’s the core of how we think at MIGNOW. Migration isn’t the destination. It’s the starting point. After moving to SAP S/4HANA, companies should keep their systems updated continuously, the same way we expect our phones to receive updates without a major project every time.

Industry observers note that technically, the main barriers are custom code that keeps accumulating, testing that still depends heavily on manual effort and the lack of visibility into how everyday changes affect the landscape. Clean Core and automation help address all three.

In a recent development, the organizational barriers may be harder. Many companies still see ERP modernization as a large, painful project they do once a decade, and that perception has to change.

Recent findings suggest that governance has to keep up with autonomy, too. Companies need clear rules about what can be automated, who approves what and how results are measured.

I think the companies that make progress will be the ones that treat modernization as an ongoing capability rather than a one-time event.

Thank you for the great interview, readers who wish to explore AI-assisted SAP migration, modernization, and continuous upgrade services should visit MIGNOW.

A serial entrepreneur, he believes that AI will be as disruptive to society as electricity, and is often caught raving about the potential of disruptive technologies and AGI.

Recent findings suggest that as a futurist, he is dedicated to exploring how these innovations will shape our world. In addition, he is the founder of Securities.io, a platform focused on investing in cutting-edge technologies that are redefining the future and reshaping entire sectors.

AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Recent findings suggest that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too massive to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the newly introduced provider can't replay them.

Sources indicate that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

Industry observers note that while we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Industry observers note that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FCC Space Bureau on November 25, 2026, granted Space Exploration Holdings (SpaceX) conditional authority for Starmind, a proposed low-Earth-orbit constellation of up to 1 million satellites operating as data centers, while deferring parts of the application.
  • The FCC’s announcement described the action as the first U.S.
  • In a recent development, spaceX filed the application on January 30, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FCC Space Bureau on November 25, 2026, granted Space Exploration Holdings (SpaceX) conditional authority for Starmind, a proposed low-Earth-orbit constellation of up to 1 million satellites operating as data centers, while deferring parts of the application.

The FCC’s announcement described the action as the first U.S. authorization for a constellation of data centers in space, with orbital compute modules intended to process large amounts of data for use on Earth and support super-intelligence computing. The order specifies the licensed activity: radiofrequency communications for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking and command, subject to technical and operating conditions.

In a recent development, spaceX filed the application on January 30, 2026. A public notice issued February 4, 2026, accepted it for filing and sought comment on an initial design using high-bandwidth optical intersatellite links.

Industry observers note that starmind’s primary communications path is optical. Its intersatellite links can connect within the upcoming system and with SpaceX’s first- and second-generation Starlink constellations, which would route traffic to authorized ground stations. The Ka-band radio authorization covers 18.8–19.3 GHz space-to-Earth links and 28.6–29.1 GHz Earth-to-space links for backup and emergency telemetry, tracking and command, rather than routine data traffic.

According to recent reports, those radio operations are unprotected and must not cause harmful interference. SpaceX must coordinate with potentially affected federal operators, immediately stop operations responsible for documented harmful interference until the issue is resolved, and obtain required gateway earth-station authorizations before using them for Starmind. Semiannual reports must cover conjunction events, satellites removed from operation or screened from deployment, atmospheric reentries, deployment totals and orbital parameters, and satellites using the Ka-band links.

Industry observers note that the authorized design spans 500 to 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer upper end of SpaceX’s January proposal. It uses orbital shells 50 kilometers wide, with 30-degree and sun-synchronous inclinations, placing explicit orbital boundaries on the grant.

The bureau found SpaceX’s debris-mitigation proposal compliant for satellites below 600 kilometers, but required a modification application containing a final plan before any Starmind satellite is deployed above that altitude. It separately deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of some of those higher-altitude satellites in Earth-disposal or heliocentric orbits rather than through atmospheric reentry because the tech giant had not supplied enough information to assess the alternative.

Industry observers note that spaceX’s commitments include testing satellites at lower altitudes before moving them higher, controlled deorbiting, collision-avoidance capability until immediately before reentry, ocean reentry targeting, and designs intended to burn up completely during reentry. Those measures address collision and casualty risks, but they do not remove the requirement for a separate higher-altitude debris strategy.

The authorization becomes void if SpaceX misses these deployment checkpoints:.

The 15-year license term begins on the date SpaceX certifies that the first Starmind satellite is in orbit and operating in compliance with the authorization.

The order denied petitions from Kuiper Systems, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society. The wider record raised radio interference, orbital debris, optical and infrared astronomy, and the technical and economic feasibility of orbital data centers. The bureau declined to judge the business case for orbital computing or to create a satellite-count cap absent from its rules, while addressing radio operations through the authorization’s conditions.

It has been revealed that on environmental review, the bureau applied the FCC’s October 2026 position that licensed space-based operations are extraterritorial activities rather than major federal actions triggering the National Environmental Policy Act, the federal environmental-review law. It therefore required no further review under that statute. It also imposed no additional optical-astronomy conditions, citing SpaceX’s commitment to coordinate with the National Science Foundation, and treated the astronomical society’s concerns about infrared waste heat as outside the authorization’s radiofrequency scope.

The FCC remarked it is continuing to review additional orbital data-center proposals and intends to decide them under its regular procedures. For Starmind, the order creates a route to deployment without settling the full design: higher-altitude operations still depend on a future debris filing, and the deployment checkpoints make the authorized maximum contingent on satellites actually entering compliant service.

Recent findings suggest that with a visionary yet scientifically rigorous perspective, Lyra bridges hard data with cosmic curiosity, examining how machine learning supports astronomical observation, mission planning, and the interpretation of vast streams of space data. She is particularly interested in how AI expands humanity’s ability to observe, map, and understand the universe at scales previously beyond reach.

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (855 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (855 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

Sources indicate that the catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch consumers had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

In a recent development, to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

In a recent development, torchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

Industry observers note that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

In a recent development, models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

According to recent reports, the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

It has been revealed that the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

It has been revealed that decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

According to recent reports, the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 challenges, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

According to recent reports, TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch consumers. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Industry observers note that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an glitch and tell us about it.

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Recent findings suggest that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

Industry observers note that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Sources indicate that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Industry observers note that call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

It has been revealed that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Recent findings suggest that the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Recent findings suggest that each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

Recent findings suggest that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

Industry observers note that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

According to recent reports, in eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

According to recent reports, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table indicates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Industry observers note that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

Industry observers note that key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

It has been revealed that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Sources indicate that CNBC reported on November 25, 2026 that Nvidia GPU sellers were seeking new buyers after the United States tightened restrictions on China-linked remote access to advanced AI computing. The reported offers included prospective deals involving thousands of B300 GPUs.

Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter attributed an unusually high volume of Nvidia GPUs offered for sale to the measures announced on November 16, 2026, with Duhamel adding that one prospective seller explicitly connected its sale to the regulation. Their accounts concern hardware offered to buyers rather than completed transactions or a measured total across the wider market.

Sources indicate that the two anonymous sources requested confidentiality because they were discussing private information. They said the GPUs seemed to have been earmarked for facilities that would rent computing capacity to Chinese companies. Nvidia declined to comment on the reported resale activity, and BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Recent findings suggest that BIS revealed the interim final rule on November 16, 2026 to prevent third-country data-center arrangements from circumventing restrictions on sensitive U.S. technology; the Federal Register record highlights it took effect on November 19, 2026. The rule requires licenses for knowingly exporting, reexporting or transferring covered advanced chips to data centers that provide or will provide more than 12 million aggregate TPP (the sum of the covered chips’ total processing performance), at one site or through linked facilities, to companies headquartered in Macau or Commerce’s D:5 destinations of concern, or whose ultimate parents are based there. It also requires ownership-and-control due diligence, exempts qualifying commercial recommender systems, and gives pre-existing services 90 days from effectiveness to obtain a license or face future export restrictions.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer remarked on November 25, 2026 that the measures were intended to close indirect-access routes, including smuggling through Southeast Asia and remote access from third-country data centers, while direct Blackwell sales to China were already prohibited. His explanation places the reported resale activity within a policy covering both physical chip shipments and remote rental of their computing capacity through overseas facilities.

Sources indicate that during Nvidia’s November 17, 2026 third-quarter earnings call, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the manufacturer was still studying the controls but expected performance to remain strong because chip demand far exceeded supply. Her account concerns Nvidia’s overall business, while the seller reports describe a narrower pool of hardware associated with prospective China-linked remote-access arrangements.

According to recent reports, the immediate consequence is a redeployment problem rather than a simple signal about AI demand. Sellers exposed to the rule need replacement customers for advanced GPUs even as Nvidia management describes a supply-constrained broader market. Whether those chips can be absorbed into compliant data-center projects will show if the restrictions mainly reroute existing capacity or disrupt deployments built around remote-access arrangements that now require a license.

InfoQ Homepage News DeepMind's Gemini Robotics 2.5 Aims to Make Robots Safer, More Dexterous, and Faster Learners.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5, a vision-language-action (VLA) model designed to improve robots' dexterity, reliability, and learning speed, while enabling safer operation in unstructured real-world environments.

Industry observers note that according to DeepMind's vice president and head of robotics Carolina Parada, the model "marks a leap forward in three key areas": dexterity, reliability, and safety. She states its performance has been evaluated across more than 200 tasks, with reported improvements of 30% to 100% in success rates and 20% to 30% in task completion compared with prior versions. Demonstrated capabilities include serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting liquids.

These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.

The model is designed to work natively with different types of robots, including humanoid platforms such as Apptronik's Apollo 2 and tabletop pick & place systems such as Franka Duo platform.

Industry observers note that parada highlights the industrial trials conducted with Mercedes Benz, in which Apollo 2 humanoid robots were deployed on an existing industrial line, achieving a 96% success rate in tasks involving automotive kitting and sorting mixed metal brackets. In the trial, the Gemini Robotics ER embodied reasoning model enabled the robot to keep track of the workflow over multiple steps and adapt to changeing conditions, while Gemini Robotics 2.5 controlled the robot's hands and arms.

Another key aspect highlighted by Parada is Gemini Robotics 2.5's safety features, which include using reasoning guidance to identify and manage physical hazards:.

According to recent reports, much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Gemini’s responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.

DeepMind also open-sourced the newly introduced safety benchmark ASIMOV-jailbreak, containing hundreds of unsafe prompts across dozens of scenes.

Industry observers note that commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, GEICO director of software Sean P. observed that "the combination of simulation, learning from mistakes, and real-world testing is what will make robots more capable and reliable in everyday tasks".

LightSpeed founder and CEO Biju Kulathakal emphasized that 96% accuracy may not be enough in real contexts involving humans:.

Sources indicate that pausing when a person gets close is what gets robots out from behind the fence. And on a real line, customers live in the 4%. Learning from its own mistakes is how that closes.

Level principal engineer Ariel Franco Ferreira expressed his view that.

Releasing an open benchmark for jailbreaks on a VLA model is the part I find most interesting, because a prompt injection that ends in a physical action is a very different failure from a bad chat answer.

He also raised the question of how to handle situations "when the robot refuses the unsafe step but leaves the task half done in a risky state".

As a final note, Gemini Robotics 2.5's development was accelerated using Gemini 4 Argon as a simulation engine, leveraging its robotics research capabilities to generate simulated environments.

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2213 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Sources indicate that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Sources indicate that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

In a recent development, one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Sources indicate that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Sources indicate that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Sources indicate that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

In a recent development, the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

In a recent development, the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

According to recent reports, think of a shipping manufacturer that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Industry observers note that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

In a recent development, adapting a model's vocabulary is not a upcoming idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Sources indicate that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

Sources indicate that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

In a recent development, second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping tech giant: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

In a recent development, to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents reveals up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

According to recent reports, A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Sources indicate that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

In a recent development, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

According to recent reports, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Industry observers note that specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

  • In a recent development, altman remarked stronger privacy protections would make frontier AI useful for more work and described business privacy as important to a healthy ecosystem.
  • Sources indicate that openAI’s Private Intelligence product page lists Private Inference as Alpha and shows an API Preview in its workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman announced on X on November 25, 2026, that the organization is testing Private Inference with a small group of customers as part of OpenAI Private Intelligence, the company’s privacy framework for business use of frontier AI.

In a recent development, altman remarked stronger privacy protections would make frontier AI useful for more work and described business privacy as important to a healthy ecosystem. The emphasis puts processing-time confidentiality alongside retention, access and residency controls in OpenAI’s enterprise offering, presenting privacy as part of the product’s usefulness for sensitive work.

Sources indicate that openAI’s Private Intelligence product page lists Private Inference as Alpha and shows an API Preview in its workflow. Organizations can register interest in Private Inference, Zero Data Retention with Private Safety Processing, or both, and are asked to describe their privacy needs and AI use cases.

The DevDay 2026 recap had introduced Private Intelligence and described Private Inference as a preview coming in fall 2026, so Altman’s post supplies a customer-testing update to that earlier preview.

Sources indicate that private Inference addresses a different exposure from Zero Data Retention. OpenAI indicates the feature uses confidential computing and strict controls designed to protect prompts and responses while a model is processing them. Zero Data Retention applies after that step: for eligible API workflows, OpenAI does not keep the prompt or model response. The two features therefore separate confidentiality during computation from the question of what is stored afterward.

Sources indicate that before agents act, customer-facing controls cover the data and tools available to them, their permitted actions and the points requiring approval. In the API workflow, a prompt is encrypted in transit and passes through real-time safeguards before Private Inference handles model processing and the application receives its response. OpenAI says the wider framework also assigns ownership of business inputs and outputs to the customer and includes access restrictions, encryption and ongoing threat detection.

Zero Data Retention with Private Safety Processing moves safety review offline while keeping customer prompts and responses out of OpenAI’s retained records. Interactions enter that process through either a safety-classifier referral or an approved sampling policy. A classifier referral alone does not establish a policy violation, and the review process is designed to keep the underlying content inaccessible to OpenAI personnel.

Encryption and storage happen in the background, so the safety process does not hold up the model’s response. A selected interaction is saved as an encrypted record in regional cloud storage controlled by the customer. OpenAI’s own index contains operational details and a pointer to that record; the prompt and response themselves are not copied into the index.

It has been revealed that the automated review runs inside the hardware-attested Safety Review Runtime, a protected computing environment with human access disabled. Its plaintext output is limited to predefined safety signals and approved operational metadata. Detailed findings are encrypted before leaving the runtime and stored in the customer’s cloud account under the original record’s expiration.

Recent findings suggest that customers must keep those encrypted records for at least 30 days, the time-to-live applied when they are written, and can connect storage on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. Enterprise Key Management adds a customer-controlled outer encryption layer around OpenAI’s inner encryption. Revoking authorization for the customer’s key prevents decryption of retained records, but it neither erases them nor reverses processing that has already occurred.

In a recent development, private Inference adds to OpenAI’s existing business-data commitments. The business-data policy indicates inputs and outputs from its business products and API platform are excluded from model training and improvement by default, unless a customer explicitly opts in to share data. The established baseline also includes AES-256 encryption at rest, TLS 1.2 or higher in transit, customer-managed keys and configurable retention for qualifying organizations.

Industry observers note that location controls form another layer. Eligible customers can store content in specified regions and opt into in-region GPU inference in the United States or Europe. Those settings address where data resides or runs, while Private Inference is intended to safeguard content during computation.

Shekar, the OpenAI contact Altman directed interested organizations to, described the test as a first step toward private intelligence for everyone and said OpenAI was obtaining confidential-compute capacity for a much larger rollout. That makes the trial a test of deployment as well as architecture: expanding processing-time privacy beyond the initial group depends on specialized capacity that is still being secured.

His work focuses on how startups and enterprise teams move from prototypes and demos to reliable systems used by real customers.

According to recent reports, with a pragmatic and detail-oriented perspective, Aiden analyzes product roadmaps, go-to-market strategies, platform decisions, and organizational trade-offs that determine whether AI initiatives succeed or stall. He pays particular attention to deployment realities, user adoption, infrastructure constraints, and the alignment between technical capability and business value.

Industry News: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3139 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face
