    Industry News: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together

    📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token.
    • According to recent reports, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck.
    • Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least key experts (in each layer independently).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.

    According to recent reports, expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency complications which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and it composes with quantization. Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.

    Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least key experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs and is important for model performance. Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.

    Our newest paper derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.

    According to recent reports, in this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers.

    Sources indicate that in a standard MoE, each layer has EEE experts, and each input token xxx is routed independently to KKK such experts ( K=8 K = 8 K=8 is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights gk(x)g_{k}(x)gk​(x) for each expert kkk, wherein the KKK experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, T(x)⊂{1,..,E}T(x) \subset\{1,..,E\}T(x)⊂{1,..,E}. The output of the layer is then ∑k∈T(x)gk(x)fk(x)\sum\limits_{k\in T(x)}g_{k}(x)f_{k}(x)k∈T(x)∑​gk​(x)fk​(x), where fk(x)f_{k}(x)fk​(x) is the output of expert kkk for token xxx.

    Recent findings suggest that left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.

    Importantly, experts in the selected set T(x)T(x)T(x) are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed before in the literature, as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.

    Industry observers note that this means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly notable, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.

    According to recent reports, this effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.

    (See Appendix A in our corresponding paper for the full derivation of the HOPE objective).

    When we delete a set of PPP experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts T(x)T(x)T(x) (for any token xxx) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set PPP (of some predefined pruning budget ∣P∣\vert P\vert∣P∣) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens xxx from our calibration set).

    Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over PPP directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set PPP itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate ZZZ, which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:.

    Z=[∑j∈P∩T(x)gj(x)∥fj(x)∥2]2≥true errorZ = \bigl[\sum\limits_{j \in P\cap T(x)} g_{j}(x)\Vert f_j(x)\Vert_{2}\bigr]^{2} \geq \text{true error}Z=[j∈P∩T(x)∑​gj​(x)∥fj​(x)∥2​]2≥true error.

    Because ZZZ is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms gi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​ between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.

    To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes E[Z]\mathbb{E}[Z]E[Z] over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:.

    P∗=arg min⁡p  p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,∑k=1Epk=∣P∣P^{*} = \argmin_{p}\; p^{\top}Fp \quad \text{s.t.} \quad p \in \{0,1\}^{E}, \sum\limits_{k=1}^{E}p_{k} = \vert P\vertP∗=pargmin​p⊤Fps.t.p∈{0,1}E,k=1∑E​pk​=∣P∣.

    where F∈RE×EF\in\mathbb{R}^{E\times E}F∈RE×E is defined as:.

    Fi,j=1∣Xi,j∣∑x∈Xi,jgi(x)gj(x)∥fi(x)∥2∥fj(x)∥2whereXi,j={x:i,j∈T(x)}F_{i,j} = \frac{1}{\vert \mathcal{X}_{i,j}\vert} \sum\limits_{x\in\mathcal{X}_{i,j}} g_{i}(x)g_{j}(x)\Vert f_{i}(x)\Vert_{2}\Vert f_{j}(x)\Vert_{2}\quad\text{where}\quad \mathcal{X}_{i,j} = \{x: i,j \in T(x)\}Fi,j​=∣Xi,j​∣1​x∈Xi,j​∑​gi​(x)gj​(x)∥fi​(x)∥2​∥fj​(x)∥2​whereXi,j​={x:i,j∈T(x)}.

    This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts iii and jjj, across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal Fk,kF_{k,k}Fk,k​ measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( Fi,jF_{i,j}Fi,j​ for i≠ji\neq ji=j) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.

    Sources indicate that what does FFF look like in practice? It demonstrates the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:.

    It has been revealed that visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.

    According to recent reports, in terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.

    Sources indicate that notably, HOPE has a strong connection to Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of FFF recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ρ=0.988\rho = 0.988ρ=0.988). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the FFF-matrix.

    It has been revealed that we evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines (REAP, MAN, EAN, and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.

    Recent findings suggest that HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.

    According to recent reports, across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.

    As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of FFF become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.

    According to recent reports, HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).

    Sources indicate that notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and has been observed across pruning methods. Furthermore, our experiments indicated that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.

    Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.

    HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix FFF. To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.

    Recent findings suggest that we created a basic package to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.

    It has been revealed that the calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.

    This command materializes the F-matrix and solves the binary quadratic program via a continuous relaxation. This takes a few seconds per layer, and the output is a JSON file which contains the prune-set. This is technically the final output of the HOPE algorithm.

    According to recent reports, to complete the pipeline, we run this command to actually create the smaller model checkpoint from the prune-set. The pruned model is a standard HuggingFace checkpoint which is smaller on disk and in memory (no changes to vLLM or SGLang model definitions needed).

    We also released a more compact Python API:.

    HOPE's advantage is most pronounced at higher pruning rates (40–50%). At lower pruning rates (10–20%), first-order methods like REAP and MAN are sometimes competitive, and HOPE's advantage shrinks. Additionally, as with most expert-pruning algorithms, HOPE prunes each layer independently and does not account for cross-layer interactions. In our paper, we presented a theoretical framework for cross-layer HOPE, but the results remain preliminary. Finally, HOPE captures pairwise interactions, but even higher-order interactions (triplets and beyond) could provide additional signal, although they are combinatorially difficult to estimate.

    For more information, see our corresponding paper and codebase.

    Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916.

    Code: https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE.

    To see how HOPE can be applied to next-generation hybrid architectures, see our corresponding repository.

    Breaking: Decision Models in Hugging Face

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2156 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text.
    • Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.
    • "I was charged twice for my subscription.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.

    Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:.

    "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.".

    The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.

    We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.

    But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?

    This is the key idea behind decision models.

    A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.

    TypeSafe AI introduced Jev, describing it as a System One model. The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).

    The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models).

    For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:.

    We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.

    However, there are a few problems with this approach.

    Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.

    Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:.

    Recent findings suggest that A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.

    The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.

    Industry observers note that if we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.

    Zero-shot classification addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.

    Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.

    One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.

    Sources indicate that this already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.

    Sources indicate that decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).

    More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.

    Consider these three approaches:.

    The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.

    A decision model request has the following two components:.

    In a recent development, the state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.

    In a recent development, questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:.

    Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.

    Which department should handle this customer request?

    The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.

    The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits z1,…,zKz_1,\ldots,z_Kz1​,…,zK​, (with KKK classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:.

    pi=exp⁡(zi)∑j=1Kexp⁡(zj) p_i=\frac{\exp(z_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{K}\exp(z_j)} pi​=∑j=1K​exp(zj​)exp(zi​)​.

    Here, KKK is the number of choices.

    Consider this illustrative distribution:.

    It has been revealed that ∑i=1Kpi=1. \sum_{i=1}^{K}p_i=1. i=1∑K​pi​=1.

    The model chooses the option with the largest probability:.

    y^=arg⁡max⁡ipi \hat y=\arg\max_i p_i y^​=argimax​pi​.

    In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.

    It has been revealed that choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?

    How urgent is this customer request?

    The model again produces a probability distribution:.

    Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.

    For a random variable XXX representing the level, the expectation is:.

    E[X]=∑i=0K−1ipi \mathbb{E}[X]=\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}ip_i E[X]=i=0∑K−1​ipi​.

    E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 \mathbb{E}[X] = 0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7 E[X]=0(0.01)+1(0.26)+2(0.72)=1.7.

    The reported score is therefore 1.7.

    In a recent development, this does not mean that the model selected a fictional level halfway between medium and high. It means that the expectation of its probability distribution is 1.7.

    The third primitive is Noul, which represents a binary question.

    Is the customer requesting a refund?

    According to recent reports, rather than defining a list of choices, we ask the model to return the probability that the answer is true. We can understand this using the Bernoulli distribution (noul comes from Bernoulli).

    Let YYY represent a binary outcome:.

    Y∼Bernoulli⁡(p) Y\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) Y∼Bernoulli(p).

    P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p. P(Y=1)=p,\qquad P(Y=0)=1-p. P(Y=1)=p,P(Y=0)=1−p.

    it assigns a probability of 0.92 to Yes and 0.08 to No.

    The model is not randomly sampling a binary answer here. It returns the probability parameter itself, leaving the application to decide how to act on it.

    So far, we have obtained probability distributions from the model. But the decision model interface also returns a field called confidence for Choice and Score.

    Recent findings suggest that the full distribution might contain several possible answers, and it is useful to summarize how concentrated the model's belief is. With confidence we achieve just that.

    For a Choice with KKK options, the confidence is:.

    pmax⁡−1K1−1K \frac{p_{\max}-\frac{1}{K}}{1-\frac{1}{K}} 1−K1​pmax​−K1​​.

    where pmax⁡p_{\max}pmax​ is the largest predicted probability.

    In our previous three-choice example, Billing had probability 0.998:.

    C=3(0.998)−12=0.997 C=\frac{3(0.998)-1}{2}=0.997 C=23(0.998)−1​=0.997.

    Notice that the winning probability is 0.998, but the reported confidence is 0.997. The confidence normalizes the largest probability relative to the number of available options. In contrast, the ordered Score example only had a confidence of 0.558.

    Decision models are a young and fast-moving space. Each one makes decisions differently under the hood (heads that score the whole schema jointly, separate readouts on top of LLM backbones, edge-sized and multimodal variants, etc). This variety is healthy, but it comes at a cost. If every model exposes its own interface, every tool around it needs model-specific adaptations.

    Our goal at Hugging Face is to agree on a common interface without forcing a common implementation. A decision model should be free to work however it likes internally, as long as it accepts the same state and questions and returns the same typed decisions. Once that contract exists, the rest of the ecosystem can build on it once:.

    The rest of this section walks through each of these pieces.

    It has been revealed that transformers now supports the DecisionPipeline, AutoModelForDecision, and the DecisionConfig classes. These follow the same overall structure of the pipeline and model classes in transformers but are tailor made for decision models.

    One can also inspect the configuration and the model like so:.

    Transformers also supports the /v1/systemone endpoint.

    We can start a local server using the serving dependencies:.

    Using a compatible version of Transformers, we can then send a decision request:.

    The response contains three named answers with the corresponding typed results and probabilities.

    It has been revealed that an interesting detail is that the above APIs works with compatible autoregressive language models too. Transformers constructs the decision prompts, evaluates the answer label logits in a batched forward pass, and applies softmax without generating response text. This means we can experiment with the decision interface without necessarily training a latest model.

    llama.cpp also supports decision models using the same /v1/systemone API.

    For example, we can launch a GGUF decision model from the Hub:.

    The default server runs on port 9931.

    Recent findings suggest that we can then send a request containing the same state and questions, using http://localhost:9931/v1/systemone. With the model selected by the server, we can omit the model field from the request.

    The useful property is interface compatibility.

    Hugging Face introduced a dedicated decision-model tag for discovering compatible models. This is useful because decision models do not have to share a single backbone or architecture.

    For example, the ecosystem includes models based on encoder architectures such as ModernBERT, as well as models derived from larger generative language-model backbones.

    In a recent development, once we understand inference, the next question is whether we can adapt a decision model. Since decision models are integrated in transformers, we can fine-tune them with the Trainer API.

    It has been revealed that below is a toy example that fine-tunes JEV-9B to route support requests. It is intentionally small, but it shows the parts that matter:.

    First-class support for training decision models is also coming to TRL (huggingface/trl#8040), so we won't have to write this plumbing by hand. At the time of writing, the PR is still open.

    If we want to go further and turn a generative LLM into a decision model, Unsloth provides a recipe that fine-tunes models such as Qwen with LoRA and a decision-scoring head.

    Decision models are interesting not because classification is latest, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

    It has been revealed that traditional classifiers already produce probabilities, and zero-shot classifiers already allow runtime-defined categories. Decision models bring these ideas into a typed interface with multiple question primitives, non-generative scoring, and the possibility of specialized training for reliable, calibrated decisions.

    In a recent development, great write-up. The step the post leaves to the application, turning noul: 0.83 into an action, is where things get hard in production. It's usually a threshold (if p > 0.9), and it quietly goes stale: raw probabilities are rarely calibrated, the right cut-off depends on what a mistake costs, and the outcome that states whether the decision was right (a chargeback, a reassigned ticket) arrives days or months later.

    According to recent reports, I'm building an open-source, self-hosted tool for that loop: trimset. It sits in front of any /v1/systemone server (so transformers serve or llama.cpp) with a one-line URL change. It logs every decision and joins the real outcome when it arrives. It calibrates per question and model, then compiles thresholds and an escalation band with a stated guarantee ("false passes ≤ 2% with 95% confidence"), which your app applies locally. It's pre-alpha; drift and silent-upgrade alerts come next.

    Live demo on recorded data, threshold simulator included: https://demo.trimset.dev/#/questions/refund_fraud/simulator.

    For anyone running decision models in production: how do you pick your cut-offs today?

    "Not because x, but because y" is very AI-sloppy language.

    According to recent reports, the advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface.

    In a recent development, nobody thinks that, literally. What I mean by that is, nothing capable of thinking would have written this sentence down because no thinking entity would suspect that decision models originated probabilistic classification. Only a non-thinking source of language, such as an LLM, might generate this sentence.

    Decision models are interesting not because classification is upcoming, but because they make decisions and probabilities first-class outputs for software.

    Again, nobody thinks that, meaning only an LLM might generate this sentence.

    The state + questions interface carries over to hosted decision models too. meraGPT Decider 1.1 takes the same shape through an API (model decider-1.1) rather than as open weights: up to 255 options per choice question, images in the state, and if you offer an "I don't know" option it takes it when the state doesn't support an answer. Against TypeSafe Jev 1.14 on the same items it's ahead on typed decisions, calibration and large label sets. Input is $0.04 per million tokens and output is free.

    Release notes: https://meragpt.com/blog/introducing-decider-1-1?utm_source=huggingface&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=hf_decision_blog.

    Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

    📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (477 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software.
    • According to recent reports, just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild.
    • Recent findings suggest that windows 10 consumers might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

    According to recent reports, just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

    Recent findings suggest that windows 10 consumers might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

    At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

    While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

    Satnam Narang at Tenable remarked the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

    “We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

    Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

    Industry observers note that tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

    “Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

    Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

    It has been revealed that heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

    On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

    As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

    The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis noted the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

    “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”.

    The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

    In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

    TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted latest “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

    Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders noted the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

    It has been revealed that “A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”.

    As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, released Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

    Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

    Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

    Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent manufacturer Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

    Industry observers note that that entity’s website — crasadr.com — claims it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

    The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

    Breaking: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site

    📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned.
    • Sources indicate that hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France.
    • In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

    Sources indicate that hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

    In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

    In a recent development, the FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

    Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

    According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

    It has been revealed that multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

    On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

    A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about latest ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

    Recent findings suggest that that source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

    KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. tech giant or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

    A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

    The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

    The following screenshot demonstrates a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology manufacturer that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

    The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

    Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).

    In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

    Industry observers note that the story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”.

    It has been revealed that mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

    According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian tech giant was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

    A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.

    According to recent reports, “If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT firm,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”.

    Recent findings suggest that an email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

    Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

    In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the organization’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

    Industry observers note that “We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”.

    The statement stated CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.

    In a recent development, it is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups right now sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.

    Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.

    According to recent reports, in December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach indicates PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).

    But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool people, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.

    A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the firm’s clients directly later on.

    The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.

    In a recent development, the following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.

    The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram speaking privately with a co-conspirator and complaining that Coveware was harming their business.

    “Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately stated they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.

    “I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.

    The operator of the ShinyHunters account on Telegram telling a co-conspirator they were “trying to eliminate the problem,” which they identified as Coveware advising victims not to pay the cybercrime group.

    Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.

    That latter dynamic, he mentioned, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.

    “It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo stated. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”.

    Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.

    “There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he stated.

    It has been revealed that in recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.

    In July, Angelo Martino, a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DOJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

    #115198. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

    Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
    • Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
    • Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up swiftly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

    Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

    Industry observers note that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

    According to recent reports, this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

    It has been revealed that pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

    In a recent development, A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

    It has been revealed that for example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

    MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

    Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

    The useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

    HierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

    In a recent development, these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

    You can make compression proportional to document length:.

    Recent findings suggest that with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

    HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

    Sources indicate that this distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

    Adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

    Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

    Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

    Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

    If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

    For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

    L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

    The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives upgrade the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

    Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

    MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

    Recent findings suggest that cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

    Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

    It has been revealed that multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

    The poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

    Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

    According to recent reports, the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

    It has been revealed that the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

    Sources indicate that this runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

    You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

    In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

    Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

    According to recent reports, sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

    Sources indicate that the default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

    Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

    In a recent development, the pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

    You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

    To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

    Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

    It has been revealed that I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

    Sources indicate that for adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

    According to recent reports, at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

    The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

    If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

    Sources indicate that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

    In a recent development, multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

    Try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

    With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

    Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today

    📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Krebsonsecurity

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers.
    • According to recent reports, the flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress.
    • It has been revealed that reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.

    Image: Shutterstock.com, Sashkin.

    According to recent reports, the flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.

    It has been revealed that reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare mentioned it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.

    OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, stated “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security challenges in recent memory.”.

    Censys, a manufacturer that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, noted a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.

    Security experts at Wiz stated every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].

    It has been revealed that “These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”.

    Sources indicate that the Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz mentioned that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.

    The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.

    According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.

    “A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”.

    Industry observers note that the SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.

    A snapshot of php2shell.censys.com, the website Censys set up to track the PHP vulnerabilities.

    Sources indicate that this is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.

    Upgrade, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
